rounds.name: A simple model of the atom

items.stem: Which statement describes what an atom is?

options.text: The smallest part of an element that can exist
The smallest particle that can ever exist
The smallest part of any compound that exists
A particle made of two or more atoms joined

items.why: This is the specification's definition of an atom.

items.stem: Which option gives the chemical symbols correctly?

options.text: So is sodium and Ox is oxygen
Na is sodium and O is oxygen
N is sodium and O is oxygen
Na is sodium, O2 is oxygen

items.why: Na represents an atom of sodium and O an atom of oxygen.

items.stem: About how many different elements are there, and where are they shown?

options.text: About 100 elements and compounds, shown in the table
About 20 elements only, all shown in the periodic table
About 100 elements, all shown in the periodic table
Many thousands of elements, most not in the table

items.why: Matches the specification: about 100 elements, shown in the periodic table.

items.stem: Which statement describes a mixture?

options.text: Two or more substances that are chemically combined
Two substances whose properties have both changed
Two or more substances not chemically combined
Two elements joined in fixed proportions by mass

items.why: A mixture consists of elements or compounds not chemically combined together.

items.stem: What were atoms thought to be like before the electron was discovered?

options.text: Tiny spheres with a nucleus in the middle
Balls of negative charge holding protons
Spheres with electrons in set orbits
Tiny spheres that could not be divided

items.why: Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be indivisible spheres.

items.stem: Which statement describes the plum pudding model of the atom?

options.text: A ball of negative charge with positive particles inside it
A ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it
A small positive nucleus with electrons around the outside
A solid sphere of matter that cannot be divided at all

items.why: This is the specification's description of the plum pudding model.

items.stem: What did Niels Bohr suggest, and how did his idea compare with experiment?

options.text: Electrons orbit at specific distances, and his calculations agreed with observations
Electrons orbit at specific distances, but no experimental observations supported this
The nucleus exists, and his calculations agreed with the observations
Electrons deflect the alpha particles, and this matched results

items.why: Bohr adapted the nuclear model, and his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations.

items.stem: What did the experimental work of James Chadwick provide evidence for?

options.text: Protons inside the nucleus, about 20 years after this was accepted
Neutrons inside the nucleus, about 20 years after it was accepted
Electrons, which had been found long before the nuclear model
The nucleus itself, at the centre of every atom

items.why: Chadwick's work showed that neutrons exist within the nucleus.

items.stem: What are the relative electrical charges of a proton, a neutron and an electron?

options.text: Proton and neutron +1, electron −1
Proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1
Proton 0, neutron +1 and electron −1
Every particle has a charge of +1 or −1

items.why: These are the relative electrical charges given in the specification.

items.stem: What does the atomic number of an element tell you?

options.text: The total of the protons and neutrons
The number of protons in each atom
The number of neutrons inside each atom
The number of electrons per shell

items.why: The number of protons in an atom of an element is its atomic number.

items.stem: What is the approximate radius of an atom?

options.text: 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m)

items.why: This is the value given in the specification.

items.stem: How does the radius of a nucleus compare with the radius of the atom?

options.text: Less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom
About 1/10 of the radius of the whole atom
About the same as the radius of the atom
About half the radius of the whole atom

items.why: The specification gives less than 1/10 000, about 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m.

items.stem: What are the relative masses of a proton, a neutron and an electron?

options.text: Proton 1, neutron 1, electron very small
Proton 1, neutron 1, electron also 1
Proton 1, neutron 1, electron 1 but negative
Proton 1, neutron very small and electron 1

items.why: These are the relative masses given in the specification.

items.stem: What is the mass number of an atom?

options.text: The sum of its protons and electrons
The sum of its protons and neutrons
The number of protons that it contains
The number of neutrons it contains

items.why: The specification defines the mass number as the sum of the protons and neutrons.

items.stem: What are isotopes?

options.text: Atoms of the same element but with different numbers of protons
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of electrons
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Atoms of different elements with the same mass number

items.why: This is the specification's definition of isotopes.

items.stem: What does the relative atomic mass of an element take account of?

options.text: The abundance of each of its isotopes
The mass number of its commonest isotope
The average of its isotope mass numbers
The number of protons and neutrons combined

items.why: Relative atomic mass is an average that takes account of isotope abundance.

items.stem: In which order do electrons occupy the energy levels (shells) of an atom?

options.text: The outer shell is filled before the inner ones
They spread out evenly between the shells
The lowest available energy level is filled first
The first shell takes eight electrons first

items.why: Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels, the innermost available shells.

items.stem: Which statement about a compound is correct?

options.text: Its elements can be mixed together in any proportions at all
Its elements keep all the properties they had before mixing
Its elements can be separated from it by simple filtration
Its elements are chemically combined in fixed proportions

items.why: Compounds contain two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.

items.stem: What must happen in every chemical reaction?

options.text: A detectable energy change must be measured
One or more new substances must always be formed
A gas or a change of colour must be seen
Two elements must join to make a compound

items.why: Chemical reactions always involve the formation of one or more new substances.

items.stem: How can a compound be separated into its elements?

options.text: Only by using a chemical reaction
By filtering it through filter paper
By evaporating the liquid away from it
By distilling the compound in a flask

items.why: Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.

items.stem: A mixture of ethanol and water is separated by fractional distillation. Which statement is correct?

options.text: New substances are made because the mixture has been heated up
The ethanol collected has different properties from before
The two liquids react with each other as they are heated
No new substances are made, as no chemical reaction happens

items.why: Separation methods are physical processes, so no new substances are made.

items.stem: Copper sulfate solution is left in an evaporating basin until crystals form. What has happened?

options.text: The copper sulfate evaporated, leaving the water behind
The water has evaporated, leaving the copper sulfate
The copper sulfate has reacted to make a blue solid
The water was condensed on a lid and collected

items.why: In crystallisation the solvent evaporates and the solute is left as crystals.

items.stem: Which statement about scientific models is correct?

options.text: New experimental evidence may lead to a model being replaced
Once a model has been accepted it can no longer be changed
A model changes when a scientist prefers a different idea
A model that explains most results is never questioned

items.why: This is the specification statement about how scientific models change.

items.stem: What conclusion came from the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment?

options.text: The positive charge is spread evenly through the whole atom
The atom is a solid ball of matter with no gaps in it
Electrons in the atom deflect the alpha particles back
The mass of an atom is concentrated at a charged centre

items.why: The results led to the conclusion that the mass is concentrated at a charged nucleus.

items.stem: In the scattering experiment a few alpha particles were deflected straight back. Why did this change the atomic model?

options.text: It showed that the whole atom is filled with positive charge
It showed that electrons are far heavier than was thought
The plum pudding model could not explain such large deflections
It proved that atoms are tiny spheres that cannot be split

items.why: A spread-out positive charge could not turn a fast alpha particle around.

items.stem: What is the main difference between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model?

options.text: In the nuclear model the mass and charge are in the nucleus
In the plum pudding model the electrons orbit a small nucleus
In the nuclear model the electrons are embedded in positive charge
In the nuclear model the mass is spread evenly through the atom

items.why: The nuclear model concentrates the mass and the positive charge at the centre.

items.stem: What did later experiments show about the positive charge of a nucleus?

options.text: It can be divided into whole numbers of identical charges
It is carried by one single particle found by James Chadwick
It comes from the neutrons, which each carry a small charge
It is spread evenly through the atom, not in a nucleus

items.why: Each of these identical smaller charges was named a proton.

items.stem: Why is almost all of the mass of an atom in the nucleus?

options.text: The nucleus takes up nearly all of the atom's volume
Protons and electrons have equal masses but opposite charges
Only neutrons in the nucleus have any mass at all
Protons and neutrons have a relative mass of 1 each

items.why: The nucleus holds all the protons and neutrons, which carry the mass.

items.stem: The electronic structure of sodium is 2,8,1. What does the final 1 tell you?

options.text: There is one electron in the third energy level
There is one electron in the innermost shell only
One of the shells in the atom is completely full
The last shell was filled up first of all

items.why: The numbers are read outwards, so the last one is the outermost level.

items.stem: Why is the electronic structure of sodium 2,8,1 rather than 2,9?

options.text: The first energy level always holds eight electrons
The second energy level holds only eight electrons
The outer energy level is always filled up first of all
The numbers are read from the outside of the atom inwards

items.why: Once the second level holds eight, the next electron starts the third level.

items.stem: Ink is spotted on chromatography paper and a solvent runs up it. Why do the dyes separate?

options.text: They move different distances with the solvent
The darkest dye always travels the furthest
The paper traps each dye as a filter would
The paper reacts with the dyes to make new ones

items.why: Each dye is held by the paper and carried by the solvent to a different extent.

items.stem: A mixture of ethanol and water is separated by fractional distillation. Why does this method work?

options.text: The two liquids boil at different temperatures
One is a solid dissolved in the other liquid
Heating the mixture makes new substances form
Water evaporates away, leaving the ethanol

items.why: Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids using their different boiling points.

items.stem: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride and hydrogen. Which is the correct word equation?

options.text: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + water
Mg + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
magnesium + HCl → magnesium chloride + hydrogen

items.why: Reactant names on the left, product names on the right, all written as words.

items.stem: A compound has the formula MgO. What is its name?

options.text: Magnesium oxygen
Magnesium oxide
Magnesium dioxide
Magnesium monoxide

items.why: The metal keeps its name and oxygen becomes oxide.

items.stem: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Which symbol equation represents this reaction correctly?

options.text: Mg + O₂ → MgO
Mg + O₂ → MgO₂
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
2Mg + 2O₂ → 2MgO

items.why: Two Mg atoms and two O atoms on each side, with the products on the right.

items.stem: (HT only) Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. Which half equation shows what happens at the positive electrode?

options.text: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + e⁻
Br⁻ + e⁻ → Br₂
Br⁻ + Br⁻ → Br₂ + e⁻
2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻

items.why: Two bromide ions lose two electrons and form a bromine molecule.

items.stem: Sand is stirred into salty water and the mixture is filtered. What is left on the filter paper?

options.text: The sand only, because it does not dissolve
The sand and the salt, which are both solids
The salty water, which stays in the paper
The salt, as filtering removes dissolved solids

items.why: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, so the sand is the residue.

items.stem: Sea water is separated by simple distillation. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Salt boils off, then condenses and is collected
Both parts boil off at different temperatures
The salt evaporates and is lost, leaving the water
Water boils off, condenses and is collected

items.why: The solvent evaporates, is condensed and collected, and the salt stays behind.

items.stem: A student wants to find out how many coloured dyes are in a sample of ink. Which technique should be used?

options.text: Filtration using filter paper and a glass funnel
Fractional distillation of the ink sample
Paper chromatography with a suitable solvent
Crystallisation in an evaporating basin

items.why: Chromatography separates the dyes by how far each one moves with the solvent.

items.stem: An atom has 11 protons. How many electrons does it have, and why?

options.text: 0, because neutrons make the atom neutral overall
23, because protons and neutrons are added together
10, because it loses one of its protons
11, because electrons and protons are equal in number

items.why: In an atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

items.stem: Two atoms each have 6 protons but different masses. What must be true?

options.text: They are atoms of different elements
They must have different numbers of electrons
They are atoms of the same element
They must have different numbers of protons

items.why: All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons.

items.stem: An atom is imagined to be as wide as a sports stadium. On this scale, about how large is the nucleus?

options.text: About the size of the whole football pitch
About the size of one of the stands
About the size of a pea in the middle
About the size of half the stadium

items.why: The nucleus radius is less than 1/10 000 of the atom's, so it is minute on this scale.

items.stem: A chlorine atom is written with mass number 35 and atomic number 17. What does it contain?

options.text: 17 protons, 35 neutrons, plus 17 electrons
35 protons, with 17 neutrons and 35 electrons
9 protons, 8 neutrons and 9 electrons
17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons

items.why: Protons = 17, neutrons = 35 − 17 = 18, and electrons equal protons.

items.stem: A chloride ion is written Cl⁻. A chlorine atom has atomic number 17. Which is correct for the ion?

options.text: 16 protons and 17 electrons, one proton lost
18 protons and 18 electrons, since it is neutral
17 protons and 17 electrons, as they stay equal
17 protons and 18 electrons, as one is gained

items.why: The 1− charge shows one extra electron; the number of protons is unchanged.

items.stem: Lithium has two isotopes: 7.5% is ⁶Li and 92.5% is ⁷Li. What is the relative atomic mass of lithium?
A magnesium atom has 12 electrons. Which electronic structure is correct?
items.why: Two electrons fill the first level and eight the second, leaving two in the third.

items.stem: A fluorine atom has 9 electrons. Which shell diagram is correct?

options.text: 2 on the first ring and 7 on the second
8 on the first ring and 1 on the second
7 on the first ring and 2 on the second
5 on the first ring and 4 on the second

items.why: The first energy level is full with two electrons, so the other seven go in the second.

items.stem: A shell diagram is drawn with 4 electrons on the outer ring, 8 on the middle ring and 2 on the inner ring. Which electronic structure does it show?
items.why: The structure starts at the innermost ring: 2, then 8, then 4.

items.stem: (HT only) Silver nitrate solution reacts with sodium chloride solution: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq). Which is the correct ionic equation?

options.text: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
Ag⁺(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s)
AgNO₃(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
Na⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq) → NaNO₃(aq)

items.why: Only these ions change; Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions and are left out.
